reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Glutaric aciduria type 1 is caused by deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase in the catabolism of lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan
Macrocephaly is frequently present at or soon after birth and should prompt consideration of the diagnosis

The cardinal risk is an acute encephalopathic crisis, usually triggered by an intercurrent illness or fasting between around 6 and 18 months, causing irreversible striatal (basal ganglia) injury and a dystonic movement disorder
Neuroimaging may show frontotemporal atrophy, widened Sylvian fissures and subdural collections that can be mistaken for non-accidental injury
Elevated glutarylcarnitine (C5DC) on acylcarnitine profile and glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acids in urine support the diagnosis, though low-excretor phenotypes exist
Distinguish from glutaric aciduria type 2 (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency), which is a separate disorder of electron transfer flavoprotein affecting many dehydrogenases
Management principles are lysine-restricted diet, carnitine supplementation, and intensive emergency treatment during illness to prevent catabolic crises
Detectable on newborn screening via elevated C5DC, and pre-symptomatic treatment substantially reduces the risk of striatal injury
reference.pathophysiology: Glutaric aciduria type 1 is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme in the degradation pathway of lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan. Deficiency leads to accumulation of glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and glutarylcarnitine. These metabolites, particularly 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, are neurotoxic and, during periods of catabolic stress, cause selective injury to the striatum, producing a dystonic-dyskinetic movement disorder. Chronic accumulation is also associated with characteristic structural brain changes and a predisposition to subdural haemorrhage. Unlike the classic organic acidaemias, severe systemic metabolic acidosis is not the dominant feature; the main threat is acute neurological injury.
additionalDifferentials: Glutaric aciduria type 2 (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency)
Non-accidental injury (owing to subdural collections and macrocephaly)
Cerebral palsy or dystonia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile with elevated glutarylcarnitine (C5DC)
Urine organic acids for glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acids
Brain MRI showing frontotemporal atrophy and widened Sylvian fissures
Molecular testing of the GCDH gene and, when needed, enzyme assay
Consideration of low-excretor status when urine metabolites are near normal
redFlags: Acute encephalopathic crisis during intercurrent illness threatening irreversible striatal injury is an emergency
New-onset dystonia, loss of motor milestones or altered consciousness in an infant
Failure to institute emergency metabolic management during fever, vomiting or poor intake
reference.prognosis: Outcome is largely determined by whether the child suffers a striatal metabolic crisis; presymptomatic detection through newborn screening with dietary treatment and emergency management can prevent the dystonic movement disorder, whereas an established crisis causes permanent and often disabling neurological injury.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting subdural collections and macrocephaly as non-accidental injury
Missing low-excretor patients whose urine organic acids appear near normal
Failing to provide aggressive emergency treatment during minor illnesses in the vulnerable age window
Assuming absence of severe acidosis excludes an organic acid disorder
management: Institute a lysine-restricted diet using lysine-free, arginine-enriched amino-acid supplements to limit production of the neurotoxic glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acids
Supplement with L-carnitine to replenish free carnitine and promote excretion of glutarylcarnitine

Implement an emergency sick-day regimen during intercurrent illness, fasting or surgery, using high-energy glucose-based feeds, temporary protein reduction and intravenous glucose to prevent an encephalopathic crisis
During the vulnerable early-childhood window, treat catabolic stress aggressively and admit promptly for intravenous glucose and carnitine when oral intake is inadequate
Manage established dystonia with agents such as baclofen or trihexyphenidyl alongside physiotherapy and supportive neurorehabilitation
Monitor growth, nutritional and carnitine status and neurological development through a specialist metabolic team and dietitian
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with newborn screening and testing of siblings for presymptomatic detection
